title: Occam's Razor
body: The principle is attributed to the 14th-century philosopher William of Ockham: do not assume more entities than necessary. It is still used as a rule of thumb for choosing the simplest explanation that fits the facts.

title: The Categorical Imperative
body: In 1785 Immanuel Kant set out a moral rule that holds regardless of one's goals: act only on a principle you could will to become a universal law. It is the cornerstone of duty-based, or deontological, ethics.

title: The Four Noble Truths
body: The core of Buddhism: life involves suffering, suffering arises from craving, suffering can end, and the way to end it is the Noble Eightfold Path. The teaching is attributed to the Buddha's first sermon.

title: I Think, Therefore I Am
body: René Descartes sought knowledge that could not be doubted and concluded that the act of doubting proves one's own existence. The argument appears in his Discourse on the Method of 1637 and became a foundation of rationalist philosophy.

title: Socrates
body: Socrates wrote nothing himself; we know him mainly through Plato's dialogues. He questioned people to expose contradictions in their beliefs. In 399 BC he was sentenced to death in Athens for corrupting the young and impiety.

title: The Five Pillars of Islam
body: The five basic duties of Islam are the declaration of faith, the daily prayers, almsgiving (zakat), fasting during Ramadan, and the pilgrimage to Mecca for those able to make it.

title: Confucianism
body: Confucius lived in China in the 6th and 5th centuries BC. His teaching stresses moral cultivation, respect within family and social relationships, and the ruler's duty to lead by example. It shaped Chinese government and culture for over two thousand years.

title: Plato's Allegory of the Cave
body: In the Republic, Plato describes prisoners who see only shadows on a cave wall and take them for reality. The allegory illustrates his view that the senses show us mere appearances, while true knowledge concerns unchanging Forms.

title: Utilitarianism
body: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill argued that the right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number. Utilitarianism is the best-known form of consequentialism, which judges actions by their outcomes.

title: The Social Contract
body: Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651), John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau (The Social Contract, 1762) explained political authority as an agreement among individuals. They disagreed on what people give up and what they keep, but the idea underpins modern theories of legitimate government.

title: Stoicism
body: Founded by Zeno of Citium in Athens around 300 BC, Stoicism teaches that virtue is the only true good and that we should focus on what is within our control. Epictetus, Seneca and the emperor Marcus Aurelius are its best-known Roman voices.

title: Existentialism
body: Jean-Paul Sartre summed up existentialism as 'existence precedes essence': humans are not born with a fixed nature but define themselves through their choices. Søren Kierkegaard in the 19th century is often seen as its forerunner.

title: Karma and Samsara
body: In Hinduism, the soul passes through a cycle of rebirth, samsara, shaped by karma, the moral consequences of actions. The ultimate goal is moksha, liberation from the cycle. Key texts include the Vedas, the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita.

title: The Great Schism of 1054
body: In 1054 mutual excommunications marked the split between the Church of Rome and the Church of Constantinople. The division into the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, rooted in disputes over authority and doctrine, persists today.

title: Aristotle's Golden Mean
body: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle argued that virtue lies between two extremes: courage, for example, between cowardice and recklessness. His virtue ethics focuses on character rather than rules or consequences.
